buyer.rubric: The budget and decision for this purchase sit with the technology and security executives who own the Kubernetes estate itself: CTO, CIO, CISO, and VPs or Heads of Engineering, Platform Engineering, Infrastructure, Cloud, Site Reliability Engineering, or Security who are accountable for keeping that estate running and compliant. Directors of Engineering, Platform, Infrastructure, Cloud Engineering, Site Reliability, Information Security or Cyber Security influence and often drive the evaluation without necessarily holding final sign-off, especially at larger enterprises where a VP or C-suite executive still approves spend. Individual contributors who feel the operational pain most acutely — platform engineers, DevOps engineers, SREs, security engineers and systems administrators — are influencers and useful signal sources, not the buyer, and should not be targeted as the purchase owner. Hard negatives are senior titles with no bearing on this purchase regardless of seniority: sales, account management, business development, partnerships, channel, customer success, marketing, HR, talent acquisition, and consulting or advisory roles, along with recruiters, freelancers and academics. The CEO is a genuine exception at smaller organisations, roughly under 1,000 headcount, where a scale-up chief executive can be a real shortcut into the decision; at larger enterprises the CEO becomes noise and the lead should instead go to CTO, CISO, VP Engineering or Head of Platform.

seller.competitorTest: A competitor in this category sells to organisations that have already centralised their certificate lifecycle and PKI governance under a dedicated third-party certificate-management platform, rather than continuing to run that discipline in-house with fragmented tools, specialist teams and manual processes.

description:
The buyers here are cloud-native enterprises and regulated institutions that run production Kubernetes at scale across distributed, multi-service architectures for business-critical digital platforms — banks, fintechs, travel and retail marketplaces, telcos, media companies, energy and pharma operators, gaming platforms, and public-sector service providers among them. The test for any candidate is not whether it happens to touch certificate or PKI tooling already, but whether the organisation itself owns the direct relationship with the end customers whose transactions and sessions run on that cluster, rather than having handed operation of that estate to a managed-service provider or systems integrator who serves those end customers on its behalf. Only the former has a buyer for this; the latter's buyer sits one layer removed, inside the MSP or SI, and is a different motion entirely. Qualifying organisations also keep an in-house engineering team that actually operates the infrastructure day to day, not one that has outsourced the whole platform.

Qualifying size runs from roughly 501 employees up through 10,000+, spanning North America, the UK and Ireland, and Continental Europe (Netherlands, Germany, France, Spain, the Nordics, Belgium, Switzerland, Austria, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Luxembourg). Below 501 headcount the infrastructure estate is rarely distributed or regulated enough to justify the spend, so that band is cold. At the very top of the range — the 10,000+ flagship consumer platforms and global banks whose engineering culture is public and whose scale matches the dream-account profile — the organisations are real fits in principle but sit behind four layers of gatekeeping; cold outbound essentially cannot reach them, so there is a practical dead zone between the reachable mid-market-to-large-enterprise band and these flagship logos, which have to be run as slow, executive-introduced named-account pursuits rather than cold pipeline. Public sector fits the profile but moves on procurement timelines that make it a named-account motion too, distinct from the charity and NGO exclusion below.

The fit spans SaaS, online retail and e-commerce marketplaces, banking and fintech, automotive, energy, pharmaceuticals, gaming, media, travel and telecoms — anywhere a regulator or a transacting customer base treats downtime as a reportable event. Excluded outright are advisory, consulting and coaching firms; marketing agencies that themselves serve this ICP; non-profits, charities and NGOs; private equity, holding companies and investment firms; architecture, planning and design firms; recruiting and staffing firms; freelancers and solo operators; and managed service providers or systems integrators who sell platform operations as a service, since they are a channel conversation rather than a direct one. Also excluded are organisations that have already delegated their certificate lifecycle and PKI governance wholesale to a dedicated third-party certificate-management platform, rather than running that discipline in-house across fragmented tools, specialist teams and manual processes — those organisations belong to a different vendor's customer base, not this one.

A platform, SRE, infrastructure or PKI role posted in the last 30 days whose description names Kubernetes, TLS, mTLS, cert-manager, PKI, HSM or service mesh is the single strongest live signal. Public evidence of production Kubernetes at real scale — an engineering blog post, conference talk, CNCF or cloud-provider case study, or public repository up to 24 months old — establishes the core infrastructure fit. Published uptime-criticality evidence, such as a live status page, a public SLA, or a real-time transactional product description, confirms the stakes are board-level regardless of page age. A regulatory or operational-resilience obligation referenced within the last 12 months — DORA, PSD2, NIS2, PCI DSS, FCA or PRA supervision, or public-sector service standards — adds regulatory pressure to the technical fit. A new platform, infrastructure or security leader appearing in seat within the last 9 to 12 months, visible via LinkedIn start date or a press release, often precedes a governance overhaul. A published post-quantum or crypto-agility commitment within the last 12 months, on a corporate blog, roadmap page or working-group listing, signals forward motion on exactly this problem. A public admission of a certificate, TLS or chain-of-trust incident within the last 90 days, surfaced in a status-page history or engineering postmortem, is a near-term trigger. An individual's public statement about certificate or PKI operational pain, posted within the last 6 months on LinkedIn, X, or in a conference talk, points directly at a motivated buyer or influencer.

requirements.text: The company operates in a vertical where a regulator or transacting customer base treats downtime as a reportable event, such as SaaS, e-commerce/retail marketplaces, banking/fintech, automotive, energy, pharma, gaming, media, travel, telecom, or public-sector services.

The company is not an advisory/consulting/coaching firm, a marketing agency serving this same ICP, a non-profit/charity/NGO, a private-equity/holding/investment firm, an architecture/planning/design firm, a recruiting/staffing firm, a freelancer or solo operator, or an MSP/SI that sells platform operations as a service.

The company has between 501 and 10,000+ employees and operates in North America, the UK & Ireland, or Continental Europe (Netherlands, Germany, France, Spain, the Nordics, Belgium, Switzerland, Austria, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Luxembourg).

The company owns the direct relationship with the end customers whose transactions and sessions run on its cluster and keeps an in-house engineering team that operates that infrastructure day to day, rather than delegating platform operation to an MSP or SI.

The company runs production Kubernetes at scale across a distributed, multi-service architecture, as evidenced by a public engineering blog post, conference talk, CNCF/cloud-provider case study, or public repository.

The company has not delegated its certificate lifecycle and PKI governance wholesale to a dedicated third-party certificate-management platform, instead running that discipline in-house across fragmented tools and manual processes.
The company has posted a platform, SRE, infrastructure, or PKI role within the last 30 days whose description names Kubernetes, TLS, mTLS, cert-manager, PKI, HSM, or service mesh.

The company has publicly referenced a regulatory or operational-resilience obligation such as DORA, PSD2, NIS2, PCI DSS, FCA/PRA supervision, or public-sector service standards within the last 12 months.
The company has appointed a new platform, infrastructure, or security leader within the last 9 to 12 months, visible via a LinkedIn start date or press release.
The company has published a post-quantum or crypto-agility commitment on a corporate blog, roadmap page, or working-group listing within the last 12 months.
The company has publicly admitted to a certificate, TLS, or chain-of-trust incident within the last 90 days, surfaced in a status-page history or engineering postmortem.
An individual at the company has made a public statement about certificate or PKI operational pain on LinkedIn, X, or in a conference talk within the last 6 months.
